topic: Walking pace vs step count: under 5,000 brisk steps matched 10,000 slow ones for mortality risk (BJSM, 100k+ UK Biobank)
angle: 'Steps AND pace: a walking cheat sheet.' In 100k+ UK Biobank adults (BJSM 2026), people who walked under 5,000 steps a day but hit a brisker peak pace (>80 steps/min) had a death risk similar to people walking 5,000–7,500 steps at a slow ~60 steps/min. 7,500–10,000 steps was linked to the lowest risk at any pace. Slides: (1) the core finding; (2) cadence guide: ~60 = leisurely, >80 = brisker (study), ~100 = moderate intensity (other research); (3) 15-second self-test: count steps ×4 to check your current pace; (4) how step count and pace combine; (5) 'observational: a link, not proof'; (6) any pace beats none, so build up gradually. Drop the 8,500-steps note unless its source is verified. Title: 'The Walking Pace Cheat Sheet: How Fast Is Fast Enough?' is fine.
title: The Walking Pace Cheat Sheet: How Fast Is Fast Enough?

topic: Stroke in younger adults: rising rates in ages 20–54 and the BE-FAST warning signs
angle: A public-service list: 'Stroke isn't just an old person's disease.' Include a slide per BE-FAST sign (Balance, Eyes, Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call emergency services), the main risk drivers (high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, smoking/drugs), and why younger adults wait too long to seek care. Quote the 'nearly doubled' figure only if the Neurology paper confirms it (the radar didn't link it). Otherwise say 'rising'.
title: Stroke Before 50: The 5 Signs That Mean Call Emergency Services Now

topic: Smartwatch calorie estimates off by 15–25% vs lab gold standard, with larger errors at higher body fat (PLOS One)
angle: 'Your watch's calories-burned number is a rough estimate.' In a small lab test (58 adults, 10 minutes of cycling), 4 popular smartwatches were off by a median of about 15–25% against a lab gas-analysis gold standard. Most overestimated, and the error grew at higher body fat. It's a small, short study, so treat it as a caution, not a verdict. Watches are better at tracking trends in steps and heart rate than exact calories. Don't extrapolate weekly calorie totals and give no eating instructions. Suggested title: 'How Accurate Is Your Smartwatch's Calorie Count? A Lab Test Checked'.
title: Smartwatch Calories Were Off by 15–25% in a Lab Test #shorts

topic: HRT pills vs patches: the '1 in 1,000' absolute risk behind the blood clot headlines
angle: A Danish registry study in The BMJ (women 50–69) linked oral HRT to a higher risk of blood clots in the legs or lungs. In absolute terms that's about [paper's figure] extra clots per 1,000 women per year. Patches and gels showed no overall increase in clot risk. The likely reason is that pills pass through the liver first. It's observational, and individual risk varies. Close with: 'Ask your clinician which route fits you, and don't stop or switch on your own.'
title: HRT pill vs patch: the blood clot number headlines skip #shorts

topic: Scented cleaners + indoor ozone create billions of nanoparticles within minutes (Purdue, ACS Fall 2026)
angle: That 'fresh clean' scent comes from terpenes such as limonene and pinene, including in 'natural' essential-oil cleaners. Indoors they react with ozone, and in Purdue's house tests the tiny particles formed could deliver a lung dose similar to standing by a busy road within about 20 minutes. Three fixes: choose fragrance-free products, run an exhaust fan while cleaning, and don't use ozone-generating 'air purifiers'. Say clearly: this is early conference data, and scientists are still working out the health effects.
title: Your "clean" smell might be polluting your air #shorts

topic: Type 2 diabetes genetic risk vs lifestyle: low ultra-processed food intake plus 150 min/week of activity linked to about 49% lower risk in people at high genetic risk (EASD 2026 abstract, 56,964 UK Biobank adults, 926 cases over 7.8 years)
angle: 'If diabetes runs in your family, is it written in your DNA?' Walk through what a polygenic risk score is, then the 3 findings: +7% risk per 10% rise in the UPF share of the diet, 39% lower risk when meeting the WHO activity guideline, and about 49% lower risk with both in the high-genetic-risk group. Explain what 'ultra-processed' means (NOVA) and why diet share isn't the same as calories. Add the practical, evidence-backed levers (guideline activity, swapping UPF staples) and link to established prevention evidence such as the Diabetes Prevention Program. Be clear on the limits: observational, a conference abstract not yet peer-reviewed, average age 69.5, mostly white UK participants, and 'linked to' not 'prevents'. Use 56,964 as the sample everywhere.
title: Diabetes Runs in Your Family? 2 Habits Linked to Lower Risk

topic: After a sleepless night, a 20-minute workout protected memory about as well as a 90-minute nap (PNAS, 53 adults aged 18–35, after 30 hours awake)
angle: After 30 hours awake in a lab, healthy young adults (n = analysed sample from the PNAS paper; coverage says 54) who did 20 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous cycling or took a 90-minute nap recognised about 56% and 57% of images on a later memory test, vs 46% for controls. EEG suggested 2 different routes: the nap reduced sleep-pressure signals, while exercise sharpened responses during learning. Then a sourced 'after a bad night' guide. Limits: small lab study, young adults, one memory task. Exercise doesn't replace sleep and doesn't make drowsy driving safe.
title: No Sleep? A 20-Min Workout Nearly Matched a 90-Min Nap on Memory Test

topic: Mammogram overdiagnosis may be under 5%, not the 30–50% often quoted (JNCI reanalysis of 8 major RCTs)
angle: 'A new reanalysis says mammogram overdiagnosis may be far lower than often quoted.' Define overdiagnosis vs false positives. topic: EASD 2026 study of 313,145 adults (UK Biobank + Copenhagen): people with a BMI of 25–26.9 and high remnant cholesterol or low-grade inflammation had heart-disease risk similar to groups who qualify for GLP-1s today
angle: 'Your BMI isn't the whole story.' Start with how GLP-1 eligibility works now: BMI thresholds plus weight-related conditions, and the SELECT population (adults with established heart disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes). Then the new finding. Among 313,145 adults, 23,134 developed coronary heart disease over 10–18 years. About 44–48% of those with a BMI of 25–26.9 had high remnant cholesterol or inflammation (CRP), and their risk looked similar to groups who are eligible today. Explain what remnant cholesterol and CRP are and how they're measured. Give the questions to bring to your doctor. Limits, said clearly: this is an observational risk study presented at a conference, it did not test GLP-1 drugs, it doesn't show that these people would benefit, and trials are needed. Avoid saying 'millions should be on GLP-1s'. Use the analysed sample size and the source's exact figures throughout.
title: Same BMI, Different Heart Risk: What GLP-1 Rules Can Miss

topic: GLP-1 hair loss: how common it is, why it happens, and what helps (BMJ Group cohort, NYU Langone study, Clinical Dermatology review Sep 2026)
angle: Keep the calm myth correction, with these changes. (1) BMJ cohort, adults with type 2 diabetes only: 1.37 times the risk vs SGLT-2 inhibitors and 1.68 times vs DPP-4 inhibitors. Label these as relative risks, say the authors call the absolute risk low, and say the hair loss was nonscarring, so it may be reversible. (2) NYU: describe it as 'a genetic study, not a study of people taking the drugs, suggested a small (~7%) added risk of male-pattern hair loss in men already genetically predisposed.' (3) Explain telogen effluvium and that it is typically temporary. (4) Levers, strongest first: enough protein, a weight-loss pace agreed with your prescriber, and asking your doctor about checking ferritin/iron, vitamin D and thyroid. (5) See a dermatologist if shedding lasts more than about 6 months, comes in patches, or is scarring or painful. No supplement promises, and don't stop the medicine without your prescriber. Title: 'Ozempic Hair Loss: How Common It Really Is and Why It Often Grows Back'. Cite the review by its exact title (e.g. American Journal of Clinical Dermatology 2026).
title: Ozempic & GLP-1 Hair Loss: How Common It Is & Why It Often Grows Back

topic: Did CagriSema beat Zepbound? REIMAGINE (type 2 diabetes) vs REDEFINE 4 (obesity)
angle: Headline decoder. 'Beats Zepbound' came from REIMAGINE 5, where CagriSema was compared with the lowest tirzepatide dose (5 mg) in adults with type 2 diabetes: 12.4% vs 9.1% at 60 weeks. In the head-to-head obesity trial REDEFINE 4 (809 adults, 84 weeks, open-label), CagriSema reached 23.0% vs 25.5% for tirzepatide's highest dose, assuming everyone stayed on treatment, and missed non-inferiority. Say on screen that this assumes full adherence. Explain amylin in one line (a satiety hormone released with insulin). The company expects an FDA decision in Q4 2026. Lesson: check the comparison group and the dose. No verdict on which drug is better, and add a talk-to-your-prescriber line.
title: Did CagriSema Really Beat Tirzepatide? #shorts

topic: Tirzepatide switched on calorie-burning brown fat, but only in obese mice

Then what human trials do show: lower appetite and 'food noise', and better blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. Add a talk-to-your-doctor line.

topic: Stopping GLP-1 medicines linked to higher heart attack, stroke and death risk: 'metabolic whiplash' in 333,000+ US veterans with type 2 diabetes (WashU)
angle: 'What happens to your body when a GLP-1 stops?' Explain why benefits seem to depend on staying on treatment, and that the effect goes beyond weight: blood pressure, cholesterol and inflammation can drift back. Walk through the study: 333,000+ US veterans with type 2 diabetes followed about 3 years; risk up to 22% higher after about 2 years off; about 18% lower risk with continuous use vs about 12% for people who restarted. Before using these numbers, check the paper for the exact outcome, the comparator for each figure, and the analysed sample. Name the limits clearly: observational ('linked to', not 'causes'); VA population, so mostly older men with T2D, and results may not apply to people without diabetes; people stop for reasons (cost, side effects, illness) that can confound the results. Evidence-based levers for anyone planning a change, strongest first: plan it with your prescriber, keep up monitoring of blood pressure, lipids and A1C (mg/dL and mmol/mol where relevant), protein, strength training and activity habits. Link to what trials show about weight regain after stopping (STEP 1 extension), with the correct population. Never say 'don't stop' or give any switching or tapering advice. Include the exact prescriber line.
title: What Happens When You Stop a GLP-1? Data From 333,000+ Veterans (T2D)
